title: Galaxy Cluster MACS J1149+2223

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble image shows the massive galaxy cluster MACS J1149+2223, about 5.3 billion light-years away in the constellation Leo. Its gravity works as a natural lens, and behind it astronomers found a galaxy that, when announced in 2012, could have been the farthest ever observed.

Gravitational lensing, predicted by Albert Einstein a century ago, happens when the gravity of foreground objects warps and magnifies light from objects behind them. This cluster brightened the remote galaxy some 15 times, bringing it into view. Its light first shone when the universe was just 500 million years old and traveled approximately 13.2 billion light-years to reach Hubble and NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope.

The galaxy is small and compact, holding only about one percent as much mass as the Milky Way, and astronomers think it was less than 200 million years old when its light set out. It dates from the era when the universe began to emerge from the cosmic dark ages, which the first galaxies likely helped to end.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's ACS and WFC3 cameras. NASA shows F435W, F475W and F555W in blue, F606W, F625W and F775W in green, and F814W, F850LP, F105W, F110W, F125W, F140W and F160W in red.
understand.eye: The total exposure time was 11.3 hours, and part of the light is infrared, which the eye cannot see.

explore: Hubble detected the galaxy in four visible and infrared bands for the CLASH cluster lensing survey, and Spitzer added a fifth, longer-wavelength band. Earlier candidates of this age had been seen in only one. Astronomers expected it to be a prime target for the James Webb Space Telescope, which was then scheduled for launch in 2018.
